extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers of fiction; literary-minded general audience
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical observations about modern novel-writing: choice of narrative voice, the balance between analysis and romance/drama, and the pitfalls of over‑dissection of character and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive minute dissection of motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of minute dissection is exercising an enormous influence in our time; the tendency of analysis to the detriment of the romantic and very often of the dramatic element in the modern novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage warns that over-analysis can turn novels into mere social history, removing romance and tragedy from private lives. Many young analysers are not successful moral anatomists and often rely on imagination rather than real insight; this can produce unnatural or unconvincing character studies. Aim to balance analysis with dramatic/romantic elements so the fiction remains alive and not merely descriptive or forensic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of narrative voice ('we' vs 'I')
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very much the custom among those who write fiction in the English language to efface their own individuality behind the majestic but rather meaningless plural, 'we,' or to let the characters created express the author's view of mankind. The great French novelists are more frank, for they say boldly 'I,' and have the courage of their opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts English writers' tendency to hide behind 'we' with French frankness in using 'I.' The remark implies an evaluative preference for authorial frankness and courage of opinion: choosing a narrative voice that carries conviction and responsibility (rather than hideous generalities) strengthens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction's mission: create and foster agreeable illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the mission of all art to create and foster agreeable illusions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit claim frames a criterion for fiction: successful art creates pleasant or convincing illusions rather than merely reporting facts. If a novel becomes only modern social history it may lose this chief merit. Use imaginative craft to produce an engaging illusion that serves emotional and aesthetic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invent tortuous motives when simplicity suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible simplicity of a strong and much tried character, good or bad, altogether escaped [the analyser]; the greatest analysers often attribute unnecessarily tortuous motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should recognize that strong characters can act from simple, straightforward motives. Avoid fabricating elaborate psychological webs where plain motives would be more believable and effective—overcomplication can paralyze action and dilute drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of relying on imagination as primary source of material
rubrics_metrics.description: We are forced to the conclusion that [many analysers] are frequently indebted to their imaginations for the results they obtain and not seldom for the material upon which they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage cautions that relying chiefly on imaginative invention (without grounding in observation or lived reality) can weaken the novel. While imagination is vital, ensure characters and motives have credible bases; otherwise the work risks vacuous or fanciful analysis rather than authentic depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve dramatic action and romance against political/social absorption
rubrics_metrics.description: The result may or may not be a volume of modern social history for the instruction of the present and the future generation. If it is not, it loses one of the chief merits which it claims; if it is, then...the political history of our times has absorbed into itself all the romance and the tragedy at the disposal of destiny, leaving next to none at all in the private lives of the actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow topical or political exposition to crowd out personal drama. Even when a novel engages with social/political change, maintain private, romantic, or tragic stakes so that the narrative retains emotional depth and the 'agreeable illusion' of art.
